copy.headline: Danish minister cleared of libelling nationalist party leader

extended.text: Frederiksberg District Court on Friday acquitted Martin Lidegaard, leader of Radikale Venstre, a social-liberal party, of libelling Morten Messerschmidt, leader of Dansk Folkeparti, a nationalist party. Messerschmidt will not appeal. He must pay Lidegaard 93,750 kroner in costs, which Dansk Folkeparti will cover.

Messerschmidt sued over three statements made at a debate in Randers, a city in Jutland, on 10 November 2025. Among them was Lidegaard's claim that 'one wants to intern and deport thousands of fellow citizens, just because they have a different faith or a different skin colour from most of us'. Lidegaard was responding to an interview in Weekendavisen, a weekly newspaper, in which Messerschmidt spoke of expelling criminal foreigners and those who cannot support themselves.

The court found the remarks capable of harming Messerschmidt's honour but backed by a sufficient factual basis. As a member of the Folketing, Denmark's parliament, Lidegaard has 'particularly far-reaching freedom of expression'; Messerschmidt, as a politician, must 'show a higher degree of tolerance'.
Lidegaard, who is also minister for business and competitiveness, called the ruling 'a completely unequivocal decision'. Messerschmidt said 'the truth has suffered a defeat'.

standard.text: Frederiksberg District Court on Friday acquitted Martin Lidegaard, leader of Radikale Venstre, a social-liberal party, of libelling Morten Messerschmidt, leader of Dansk Folkeparti, a nationalist party. Messerschmidt will not appeal and must pay 93,750 kroner in costs.

At a debate in Randers, a city in Jutland, on 10 November 2025, Lidegaard said that 'one wants to intern and deport thousands of fellow citizens, just because they have a different faith or a different skin colour from most of us'.

The court found a sufficient factual basis for the remarks. As a member of the Folketing, Denmark's parliament, Lidegaard has 'particularly far-reaching freedom of expression', and Messerschmidt must 'show a higher degree of tolerance'.

Messerschmidt will not appeal and must pay 93,750 kroner in costs.

copy.headline: Trump suspends Russia sanctions days before they take effect

standard.text: Donald Trump on Friday suspended a range of sanctions, restrictions and tariffs on Russia, days before they were due to take effect, telling Congress that the exemption was 'in the US national interest'.

They come from a law Trump signed in mid-September, named after Lindsey Graham, a Republican senator who died in July. It would have put tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods from the five biggest importers of Russian oil or gas. India, among the largest buyers, had voiced concern.
Trump has announced a deal for Russia to deliver almost five million tonnes of diesel to America, and has suggested Ukraine needs a new leader.

short.text: Donald Trump on Friday suspended a range of sanctions, restrictions and tariffs on Russia, days before they were due to take effect. The law he signed in mid-September would have put tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods from the five biggest importers of Russian oil or gas.

copy.headline: Denmark's oldest person confirms she joined the Danish Nazi party in 1941

standard.text: Kirsten Schwalbe, who on Wednesday became the oldest person ever to have lived in Denmark, joined DNSAP, the Danish Nazi party, in August 1941, during the German occupation. On Friday she confirmed that she and her late husband had both been members, but would say no more.
Two historians found her in the Bovrup file, a copy of the party's own membership register published after the war.

TV Midtvest, a regional broadcaster that has followed her for four years, says it did not know. Bent Blüdnikow, a historian, told Kristeligt Dagblad that membership 'was treason', though it was not made a crime in itself after the occupation.

short.text: Kirsten Schwalbe, who on Wednesday became the oldest person ever to have lived in Denmark, has confirmed that she joined DNSAP, the Danish Nazi party, in 1941, during the German occupation.

copy.headline: Funen man is charged with abusing 68 children online

standard.text: Prosecutors have charged a 25-year-old man from Funen, a Danish island, with grooming 68 children and with sextortion, in which an offender threatens to publish the victim's pictures or films. Most were between 11 and 14. He denies the charges. His trial opens on Tuesday in Svendborg, a town on Funen, and a verdict is expected in December.

According to the indictment, he contacted the children on Snapchat and OmeTV, which police call a chat roulette, and got them to perform sexual acts on themselves while he watched on screen. Police have identified 27 of the 68, most from Denmark. He has been in custody since March 2025.

copy.headline: EU leaders tell the Commission to find money for Ukraine in 2027

standard.text: EU leaders asked the European Commission on Friday to propose how to close Ukraine's budget gap for 2027, said António Costa, president of the European Council, after the summit in Brussels. Ukraine puts its financial and military shortfall at 70 billion euros or more.
Last year 24 of the 27 EU countries, Denmark among them, agreed to borrow 90 billion euros for Ukraine for 2026 and 2027; the G7 and the IMF, which were to cover the rest, are slow to pay.
Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister, points to frozen Russian assets. Belgium, where most are held at Euroclear, a securities depository, refuses for fear of a Russian lawsuit.

short.text: EU leaders asked the European Commission on Friday to propose how to close Ukraine's budget gap for 2027, which Ukraine puts at 70 billion euros or more. Belgium still refuses to use frozen Russian assets.

copy.headline: Minister refuses to let a calculation error delay Denmark's new limits on farm fertiliser

standard.text: Christian Rabjerg Madsen, the minister for nature and animal welfare, will not let a calculation error at Aarhus University delay stricter limits on farm fertiliser, due from 1 January 2027. 'The consequence of waiting is simply more oxygen depletion, more algal slime and more dead fish,' he told Ritzau, the Danish news agency, on Friday.

His government partners, the Moderates, a liberal party founded by Lars Løkke Rasmussen, a former prime minister, had said the start date might be revisited. The university admitted the errors after several inquiries from Seges, a farming think tank. SF, a left-wing party also in government, opposes any delay.
